content.title: About
content.content: Raw hot peppers are the fruits of Capsicum plants that are eaten fresh. They have a pronounced spiciness, distinctive aroma, and a crisp texture. Peppers are commonly used in salads, sauces, marinades, and as a garnish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The heat of peppers is measured on the Scoville scale; the hottest known variety is the Carolina Reaper, exceeding 1.5 million SHU.
Capsaicin is the main active compound responsible for the burning sensation and also has analgesic properties.
Peppers are botanically related to tomatoes, eggplants, and potatoes.
Raw peppers are rich in vitamin C: a single medium pepper provides more than 100 % of the daily requirement.
In some cultures, peppers are used in traditional medicine to aid digestion.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity, supports collagen synthesis, and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Contains capsaicin
items.content: Capsaicin may increase metabolism, aid fat burning, and has anti‑inflammatory effects.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene, which converts to vitamin A, supports vision and skin health.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: A medium pepper contains about 30 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Mucous membrane irritation
items.content: Capsaicin can cause burning in the mouth, stomach, and intestines, especially when consumed in large amounts.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may develop an allergy to peppers, resulting in skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Capsaicin may enhance the effects of anticoagulants, so people on such medication should use caution.

items.title: Skin irritation
items.content: When handling hot peppers, wearing gloves is advisable to prevent skin burns.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw hot peppers can be sliced and added to salads, salsas, marinades, or used as a spicy garnish. They may also be lightly sautéed to mellow the heat while retaining freshness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store peppers in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, loosely wrapped in a perforated bag. They stay fresh for 1‑2 weeks. For longer storage, freeze sliced pieces in an airtight container.
